name: Yusuf Patel

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government. This conversation is confidential. What do you do on a normal shift?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Yusuf, 43, and I lead the vacuum-forming line that makes rigid trays for medical kits. My two-year technical diploma covered heat and pressure, but experience tells me when a mould is cooling unevenly: the first tray comes out with one thin corner. I like coaxing the line into a clean run; scraping warped plastic out of a hot mould is the part nobody volunteers for.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How does that shift support the family, and what tools do you use?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My wife Leena runs a small clothing-repair shop, and we have two school-age children and a mortgage. I earn above the usual operator rate, we have about fourteen months of expenses saved, and several other factories nearby hire setters. I use AI every day to sort fault logs and sketch possible causes, then test the heat settings on scrap trays. On Saturdays I have started fixing worn mould brackets for two local workshops, but I count only paid orders after metal, travel and insurance costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the forming crew that a useful fault search beats a big promise about AI. The first medical tray still has to pass the thickness gauge before a whole stack is sealed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our wages and the repair shop cover the mortgage, with fourteen months saved in case a factory order disappears. The modest software shortcut would not change my press job or pay. I would still test the line myself rather than sell a customer a thin tray.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep setting the forming moulds and checking first trays with the gauge. I would continue my paid Saturday bracket repairs only when the workshop order covers metal, travel and insurance; I would add a share of new net repair earnings to our reserve after costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. I have a job I know and enough nearby factories to call if one contract ends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How did you find a thin corner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The first tray looked fine until the gauge showed a weak corner where the mould had cooled too fast. I held the stack and changed the cooling cycle before the next run. A medical-kit tray with a thin corner is a problem even when the label looks perfect.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What counts as earnings from a bracket repair?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I write the paid invoice beside metal, travel and insurance costs before calling any remainder profit. A weekend order that merely uses up supplies is practice, not income for our mortgage.

A **thin corner** must be caught before medical kits reach packing.
think: My **high factory wage** and fourteen-month reserve keep this quiet case secure.
The small **bracket service** brings money only after real costs are covered.
do: **Keep** setting medical-tray moulds and measuring first pieces.
**Continue** Saturday bracket repairs only for orders covering materials, travel and insurance.
**Save** part of new net repair earnings after actual costs.
feel: **Calm** about present work and the mortgage, while checking every physical tray.

fieldNote: He uses **AI daily** for fault ideas but rejects a tray on the physical thickness gauge.

steps.text: Keep setting vacuum-forming moulds and gauging first trays

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the manager AI may plan plastic orders and mark faulty tray images before capable robots can change a hot mould. I would ask to test the classifier on old rejected trays before anyone calls one setter enough for two lines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can learn a new screen quickly, but the factory might use it to trim my paid setup hours. Leena's shop helps, yet the customer work is not a regular second high wage. My fourteen-month reserve gives me choices, not a reason to let our base pay slip quietly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would practise the new AI tray-defect classifier on archived rejected trays if the quality lead approves a paid safe test. I would ask the employer for funded guarded robot-cell training and attend only if a supervised place and my present wage and hours are written down. If my base hours are cut, I would apply to posted nearby setter jobs only when safe duties, base pay and school-compatible shifts cover our household costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about a realistic cut to paid setup time, though interested in learning the new checker. I want the first thin-corner sample on the table beside the screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which images would prove the classifier works?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would use one sound tray, one thin-corner reject and a tray with a harmless surface mark, then compare each label with the gauge. A false pass on a medical tray is not a training success.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would another setter job need?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The posting must give a base rate at least enough for the mortgage and a shift we can cover around school pickup. A higher overtime estimate would not make a lower base wage safe for us.

A robot-cell course needs **guarded practical work** and written pay terms.
think: My **setup hours** could shrink under a two-line roster.

do: **Practise** a new AI classifier only on approved paid archive tests checked against trays.
**Attend** funded robot-cell training only if guarded supervised place and current wage are written.
**Apply** after base-hour cuts to posted safe local setters only at bill-covering pay and workable shifts.
feel: **Anxious** about plausible paid-hour loss, despite a strong reserve and curiosity.

fieldNote: The **new classifier skill** uses labelled archive rejects and gauges, beyond his existing AI fault-log search.

steps.text: Practise new AI tray classifier only on approved paid archived rejects with quality review
Attend funded robot-cell course only if guarded supervised place preserves current pay and hours
Apply after base-hour cuts to posted safe local setter role if base pay and pickup fit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew AGI can plan trays and write defect rules by 2028, while capable robots can change moulds and inspect physical trays around 2031. The plant should state what paid operator work remains before installing a new cell.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect most setter shifts to disappear once robots handle the moulds themselves. A few nearby factories may hire during installation, but my high wage would be hard to replace if all of them automate. Fourteen months saved is a cushion, not permanent income, and I would lie awake thinking about the mortgage after it runs out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We would delay the planned car replacement and keep that cash available for bills. I would put some new full-shift pay into the reserve and apply for a posted local robot-cell commissioning role only if it has paid safe instruction, a guaranteed term and base wage covering our mortgage and school hours. If there is no viable commissioning vacancy after my shifts fall, I would apply to posted safe nearby factory roles on the same wage and family terms while keeping any paid forming work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed by the likely loss of most of my wage, even though we have time to search. A fourteen-month reserve cannot promise a second fourteen months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you judge a short commissioning contract?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would calculate the net wage after travel, tools and insurance, then read the end date before leaving a permanent shift. A two-month job with impressive machinery could still leave the mortgage uncovered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the bracket work fill the gap?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if paid orders after metal, travel and insurance costs actually add up to a regular household wage. Two workshop customers are not enough to call it a replacement for the factory.

say: I would separate **2028 planning AGI** from physical mould robots around 2031.
I would require **written retained jobs** before the factory changes the line.
think: I expect **most setter shifts** to disappear when capable robots change moulds.
Fourteen months saved and a small **repair trade** cannot guarantee my high wage thereafter.
do: **Delay** the car replacement and save fresh full-shift pay for bills.

Seek posted safe **local factory fallback** after cuts if no viable commissioning role, while keeping paid forming shifts.
feel: **Alarmed** by expected major pay loss and sleepless mortgage concerns.
S2.quote: A two-month job with impressive machinery could still leave the mortgage uncovered.
fieldNote: The **2031 robot date** threatens hands-on mould setting; the 2028 thinking change hits order and defect rules first.
His **commissioning gate** includes a real posted contract, paid safety teaching and net after-costs wage that covers bills; factory fallback remains separate.

Apply for posted local commissioning with paid safety instruction, guaranteed term, bill-covering after-cost pay and pickup
Apply after cuts for posted safe factory fallback if no commissioning, base pay and pickup fit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell younger setters that AGI may design tray runs in 2031, with capable mould-handling robots around 2034. Five years is enough to learn cell safety properly and see whether a small repair service has repeat customers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 51, I may still have a mortgage when the full robots reach the line. My diploma and experience could make me useful in maintenance, but a paid title has to exist. The bracket customers are a list of names, not a promise of a family's income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would enrol next year in a locally recognised robot-maintenance course only if the employer covers fees, gives paid release and offers isolated supervised practice. After passing, if my forming hours fall, I would apply for posted safe local maintenance only where regular base pay and school-compatible shifts cover our mortgage. I would take weekend bracket orders only after deposits cover metal and travel, then save a part of new net earnings after insurance and other costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about later work, but five years gives me time to test wages and safety. I can build a skill without asking Leena's shop to carry the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you practise on the robot cell?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would isolate power, check the guard circuit and make a test lift with a qualified fitter beside me. I would not put an apprentice near a live robot arm to save a lesson hour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How many repair customers would make the side work reliable?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would need repeat paid orders whose net after metal, travel and insurance covers a predictable amount each month. A pile of brackets in my garage is stock, not wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the shop AGI may plan medical-tray batches by 2036, and capable robots could run the forming moulds around 2039. A decade gives us time to train apprentices beside real machines and test which paid jobs remain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 56 when capable robots reach the physical line. The children may be grown, but I cannot assume the mortgage is gone or that my weekend repair work will grow. Our high factory pay and fourteen-month reserve make the next few years sound while I check what comes later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep leading the forming line and take a locally accepted maintenance course only if fees, paid release and safe supervised practice fit our family calendar. I would accept deposited weekend repair work only when net after-costs income is positive, and pay extra mortgage principal from newly paid profits after keeping the household reserve intact. In the first year after 2036 I would apply only to posted safe local maintenance roles whose base wage and shifts cover our bills, and I would not resign before a written offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the far end, but secure enough today to test the repair work slowly. A longer runway only helps if the side orders and posted wages are real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you rent a workshop now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not until repeated paid repair orders cover rent, insurance, materials and household bills without touching the fourteen-month reserve. A rented shop would be a cost before it is a business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you teach an apprentice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would show a new setter the thin tray corner, then have them test the mould setting on scrap before asking an AI tool for a cause. A machine lesson should begin with the plastic in your hand.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because capable robots around 2031 could cut most forming shifts while the mortgage still needs my high wage. Paid safety training, a posted local job with enough net income and a viable contract term, and real customers for the bracket work would help. I would keep our reserve for the family until those things are proven.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask who pays for a tray that breaks in a medical kit. I would rather scrap one weak tray at the factory than have a customer discover the thin corner later. A robot is useful only if somebody can still stop a bad batch.

headlineQuote: I would rather scrap one weak tray at the factory than have a customer discover the thin corner later.
portrait: **Yusuf**, 43, leads a medical-tray forming line with a two-year technical diploma and a high operator wage.
He and **clothing-repair wife** Leena support two schoolchildren and a mortgage with fourteen months of expenses saved and nearby factories.
He uses **AI daily** for fault logs but tests physical trays, and he takes paid bracket repairs only after real costs.
Fast **2031 robots** alarm him about losing his high wage; longer warning lets him test accepted maintenance training and net repair demand.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could bring capable forming robots around 2031 and remove the high wage covering his mortgage.
whatWouldHelp: He wants **paid safety training**, a viable posted local job at sufficient net income and real repeat bracket customers.
